title: One CPU, two requests
intro: A small schedule shows how I/O waiting can overlap useful CPU work. Times are illustrative milliseconds.
roles: Tasks that can run wait here until the scheduler selects them.
Only one task computes at a time on this single CPU.
A blocked task waits for an external event and does not consume CPU here.
A task completes only after its CPU and I/O phases finish.

steps.label: Both requests arrive
steps.detail: A and B each need 10 ms of CPU, followed by 90 ms of I/O.

steps.label: Run A
steps.detail: A uses the only CPU for 10 ms. B remains ready.

steps.label: A blocks; run B
steps.detail: A waits for I/O until time 100. B can now use the CPU.

steps.label: Both wait
steps.detail: B starts its own 90 ms wait. The CPU has no runnable request.

steps.label: A finishes
steps.detail: A’s I/O completes at 100 ms. B still waits until 110 ms.

steps.label: B finishes
steps.detail: Both requests complete in 110 ms, rather than 200 ms if run strictly sequentially.

limit: Assume independent I/O, no contention, zero scheduling overhead, and no final CPU phase. This is concurrency, not simultaneous CPU computation.

title: Cumulative acknowledgments and a lost segment
intro: Follow three byte ranges. ACK values name the next byte the receiver needs.
roles: The sender retains unacknowledged data so it can retransmit it.
This example deliberately loses one segment. Real networks can also reorder or duplicate packets.
The receiver exposes ordered bytes to the application. This example buffers out-of-order bytes.
A cumulative ACK confirms a contiguous prefix and identifies the next missing byte.

steps.label: Send bytes 0–99
steps.detail: The first 100 bytes reach the receiver.

steps.label: ACK 100
steps.detail: The receiver has a contiguous prefix through byte 99.

steps.label: Lose bytes 100–199
steps.detail: The next segment is lost in transit.

steps.label: Bytes 200–299 arrive
steps.detail: Later bytes do not close the gap. The receiver still cumulatively acknowledges only the prefix.

steps.label: Retransmit the gap
steps.detail: After loss detection, the sender retransmits bytes 100–199.

steps.label: ACK 300
steps.detail: The gap closes. Bytes 0 through 299 now form one contiguous prefix.

limit: Byte numbers start at zero for teaching; connection setup and sequence-number wraparound are omitted. This trace does not prescribe a specific loss-detection algorithm.

title: Two buyers, one remaining item
intro: A guarded write protects inventory even when both buyers initially see the same value.
roles: A read alone does not reserve inventory. Another transaction can observe the same count.
An atomic conditional update changes inventory only if a positive count remains.
A successful transaction makes the reservation durable under the database’s commit guarantees.
Zero affected rows means the precondition failed; the application must handle that outcome.

steps.label: Both observe one item
steps.detail: A and B read stock=1. Neither read reserves it.

steps.label: A wins the conditional write
steps.detail: A executes UPDATE inventory SET stock=stock-1 WHERE id=7 AND stock>0.

steps.label: A commits
steps.detail: A’s transaction commits its reservation.

steps.label: B checks the precondition
steps.detail: B’s conditional update finds stock=0 and changes no row.

steps.label: Report sold out
steps.detail: B must not create a successful reservation from its stale initial read.

limit: Illustrates an atomic guarded-write design. Exact waiting, visibility, and retry behavior depend on the database and isolation level; multi-row invariants need additional design.

title: TTL expiration meets LRU ordering
intro: Capacity is two entries. Order is shown from most recently used to least recently used; an entry expires at now >= expires.
roles: The API defines get/put behavior, absence, expiration, and eviction.
The map locates each entry and its linked-list node.
Successful access moves a live entry to the front. Eviction removes the least recently used live candidate.
The injected clock makes the equality boundary deterministic and testable.

steps.label: Insert A
steps.detail: At time 0, store A with expiry time 5.

steps.label: Insert B
steps.detail: B expires at time 10; capacity is now full.

steps.label: Read A at time 4
steps.detail: A is still live, so return its value and move it to the front.

steps.label: Read A at time 5
steps.detail: The equality boundary means A has expired. Remove it from both map and list.

steps.label: Insert C, then D
steps.detail: C fills the spare slot; D then evicts B, the least recently used entry.

limit: This is a sequential trace with lazy expiration. Production concurrency, background cleanup, and clock behavior need explicit contracts.

title: Token bucket under a burst
intro: Capacity is 3 tokens and refill rate is 1 token per second. Each admitted request consumes one token.
roles: The gateway identifies the quota key and applies a known policy.
Refill and consume must act atomically for the same bucket; otherwise concurrent callers can overspend.
An allowed request consumes one token before entering the protected service.
A rejected request must follow the API’s retry contract; retries also need a bound.

steps.label: Full bucket
steps.detail: At time 0, the bucket contains its capacity of three tokens.

steps.label: Admit the first request
steps.detail: Consume one token.

steps.label: Admit two more
steps.detail: Three requests at the same instant consume the full burst allowance.

steps.label: Reject the fourth
steps.detail: No token remains at time 0.

steps.label: One second passes
steps.detail: Refill one token, capped at capacity. One new request can be admitted.

steps.label: Idle until time 5
steps.detail: Refill is capped at 3; the bucket never grows without bound.

limit: One quota key, an authoritative monotonic clock, and atomic updates are assumed. This does not implement a distributed consistency protocol.

title: RAG: relevant does not always mean usable
intro: Trace a query against two public documents and one restricted document. Authorization is part of retrieval.
roles: The request carries the caller’s identity and permission scope.
Retrieve candidate evidence under the caller’s access rules.
Rank usable passages and fit them into the context budget with stable document IDs.
Generate only claims supported by the selected evidence; check citations and handle insufficient evidence.

steps.label: Ask about the retry limit
steps.detail: The caller can read documents A and B, but not restricted document C.

steps.label: Retrieve usable candidates
steps.detail: A says retries are capped at 3. B describes backoff. C must not enter the model context.

steps.label: Build the evidence context
steps.detail: Keep the supporting passages and their document identifiers.

steps.label: Answer with support
steps.detail: Answer that the documented cap is 3 and cite A. Do not invent the total deadline if the evidence does not state it.

steps.label: Evaluate the result
steps.detail: Check that the cap is supported, the citation points to A, and no restricted content leaked.

limit: A deterministic example of a retrieval pipeline, not a live model call. Ranking quality and answer support still need a representative evaluation set.
